content:
Originally estimated around 2,145 trees will be felled

The project is currently undertaken by a joint venture of "China State Construction Hong Kong", "Aitken" and "China State Construction Civil Engineering". According to a 2024 Legislative Council document, there are approximately 2,270 trees within the project scope, and around 2,145 are expected to be felled, including 10 "trees of special value" — Aquilaria sinensis (Incense Tree) and 2 Ormosia henryi. The authorities plan to replant approximately 2,140 trees after completion, including Koelreuteria bipinnata (Golden Rain Tree), Magnolia grandiflora (Southern Magnolia) and Michelia champaca (Yellow Champaca), among others.

Loss of shade from large trees — Residents: Heat feels even more intense in hot weather

Reporters recently inspected the area from Marina Cove to Sai Kung Town Centre and found that trees had been removed along roads at Pak Wai, Marina Cove, Hiram's Bay, Pak Kong and Sai Kung Town Centre. Felling is particularly noticeable around Pak Kong — as levelling works are underway, by the reporter's visual estimate, nearly one-third of trees on the hillside have been cut down; at least 15 consecutive trees have also been felled alongside the road at Tai Chung Hau Village. Villagers said that with the roadside greenery diminishing, the heat feels even more oppressive during very hot weather.

Levelling works are underway on the Pak Kong hillside, with trees being felled on the slope.

A hole was drilled into a felled large tree, with a bottle of orange juice placed inside.

Removal of approximately 1,900 trees unavoidable

In response to enquiries from "集誌社" (Stand News), the Highways Department said that because the relevant works run very close to vegetation-covered slopes on both sides of the road, some trees — mainly situated on the slopes — have to be removed or transplanted to free up sufficient space for the works. After investigation, the unavoidable removal of approximately 1,900 trees remains necessary.

13 Aquilaria sinensis — 11 expected to be felled

The authorities said there are 13 Aquilaria sinensis within the project scope. After examining their shape, structure and growing location, 11 are considered unsuitable for transplantation and have to be removed, with the remaining 2 retained in situ. One Ormosia henryi, after examination, is also considered unsuitable for transplantation and has to be removed; one camphor tree originally slated for transplantation has, after examination, to be removed. Three Indian Banyan trees are retained in situ.

The authorities said the project team will plant approximately 2,000 trees at suitable locations within Sai Kung District, such as roadside greening belts, to enhance the roadside landscape and the Sai Kung community environment.

Aquilaria sinensis is classified as Vulnerable

Aquilaria sinensis is a native Hong Kong species, mainly distributed in Sai Kung, the northeastern New Territories and on Lantau Island. As of 2021, there were approximately 5,000 mature Aquilaria sinensis trees across Hong Kong. The species is classified as rare, and is listed as a protected plant under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance, as well as being listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Because its resin can be refined into the precious fragrance "agarwood", in the early years — especially around Sai Kung — there were mainland "tree-felling gangs" who came to Hong Kong to illegally log the trees, with black-market prices exceeding HK$10,000.

As for Ormosia henryi, it is an evergreen tree of the genus Ormosia (family Fabaceae, subfamily Papilionoideae), listed by the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department as a rare and precious plant. The species was first discovered in Happy Valley in 1850, and is now classified as Endangered within China.

Pak Wai Village resident Regina bought a village house years ago. A self-styled "flower fanatic", her decision to buy the house was entirely down to an old tree in front of the property, which she likens to a "treasure". Upon learning of tree-felling in the surrounding area, she said emotionally: "It's 2,000 trees, not 200!" She believes Sai Kung has long enjoyed the reputation of being "Hong Kong's back garden", and questions: "Without those 2,000 trees, can Sai Kung still be called Hong Kong's back garden?"

Regina, a self-styled "flower fanatic", decided to buy her home in Sai Kung entirely because of an old tree growing in front of the house, which she describes as finding a "treasure". (Provided by Regina)

She said trees have life, and may even take a century to grow; once lost, they are hard to recover — including the precious Aquilaria sinensis. Taking Pak Wai Village as an example, she pointed out that tourists may not remember the village name, but they remember an old tree at the village entrance — so much so that it has become a bus stop landmark. "I can see that mountain precisely because of these trees; try having no trees, how would I see the mountain?" She believes the Government should not take a one-size-fits-all approach and sacrifice nature conservation.

Residents deeply attached to old trees

Another Sai Kung resident, Amy, said three generations of her family, including her children, all grew up in Sai Kung. "Seeing the trees gone, all those years of growing up are gone too." Spectacles-free, she joked that all these years she has had excellent eyesight precisely because of the surrounding greenery and the green woods in the distance — "Suddenly they cut them down, and even the kids will have to wear glasses".

Beyond witnessing the disappearance of trees, she lamented the changes she has seen in Sai Kung over the years — for instance, the many historically significant buildings opposite Clear Water Bay Road, including the 1946-built "Chung Hwa Paint" factory — known for its "Chrysanthemum", "Giraffe" and "Toy" brands — which is to be demolished and redeveloped into residences. She also cited the recent example of a strong typhoon bringing down an old tree in the town, which drew residents to take photos, reflecting residents' deep emotional attachment to old trees.

Roadside scenery has become "eyesore"

Sai Kung resident Mr Tam said that although he does not know the exact number of trees felled, it is plainly obvious that trees along the route have dwindled. "There used to be so many trees, it was very pleasant — now you see this mess, it's uncomfortable." He said when he moved to Sai Kung one to two years ago, large-scale felling had not yet begun; the cutting of Aquilaria sinensis, he also finds a pity. He also questioned whether road widening would help relieve congestion: "Going into Sai Kung on holidays, you expect traffic jams anyway".

An 84-year-old Sai Kung resident known as "Uncle" has lived in the district for more than 20 years. He said that since more than a thousand trees were felled, the Sai Kung landscape has become unrecognisable, questioning: "What's the connection between traffic jams and those trees? Your cars don't go through the trees, do they".

Friends of the Earth Director Wong Cheuk-yuet said that when project consultants assess trees, although it may not be deliberate, to facilitate construction it is easy to fall into a "picking bones from an egg" situation — "if it can't be moved, cut it down" — rather than trying to save each tree one by one. For instance, ordinary species of trees almost need to be "perfect" to be retained; even if a tree is in fair condition, as long as it has a minor defect or its growing space is slightly inadequate, the report will list adverse factors; large trees may require transplantation costs easily exceeding a million dollars, or may deteriorate due to procedures or the difficulty of finding a suitable location to accommodate them.

Aquilaria sinensis should in principle be preserved as far as possible

He acknowledged that some locations in Sai Kung are on slopes, making excavation of root balls and transplantation more difficult, but if conservation is the goal, heavy crown pruning, reducing root-ball size and so on should be considered, with "preserving the species" and "saving its life" as the primary objectives. With the number of Aquilaria sinensis having dropped significantly, they should in principle be preserved as far as possible. He is also concerned that, with additional traffic lanes and separation barriers added to the road, there will be insufficient space for planting along the route, turning what was once a shady corridor into large expanses of concrete, which in the long run may affect the experience of waiting for and walking to public transport.
